RECOTA combines physical optics, physical theory of diffraction, ray tracing, and semiempirical formulations for RCS calculation.
Target geometry is modeled as facets and wedges using a CAD package, allowing detailed and flexible shape representation.
Shadowing, multiple scattering, and discontinuities are explicitly accounted for in the RCS computations.
The body of revolution technique is limited to simply shaped targets made of or approximated as bodies of revolution.
The method of components technique breaks complex targets into primitives like cones, cylinders, and flat plates for RCS estimation.
Physical optics predicts uniform currents on facets, while physical theory of diffraction accounts for edge currents on wedges.
Shadow region calculations identify self-shadowing and mutual shadowing by projecting facets onto a plane perpendicular to radar line of sight.
Multiple scattering is approximated by considering facet-facet interactions with ray-tracing phase delay calculations.
Discontinuities such as slots and screws are modeled as line segments and included via semiempirical scattering formulations.
RECOTA was verified experimentally using NACA airfoils and conducting spheres, showing good agreement with measured RCS data.
For NACA 3317 airfoil at 16 GHz, RECOTA predictions matched measurements within 1-2 dBsm for horizontal polarization.
Vertical polarization RCS predictions improve with increasing electrical size parameter ka, reducing discrepancies from 3 dBsm to about 1 dBsm.
The faceting approach may require many facets, increasing computational time and memory, but is suitable for component-level analysis.
RECOTA assumes monostatic RCS for perfectly conducting bodies under high-frequency conditions where wavelength is small compared to target size.
The overall scattered field is computed as the sum of contributions from facets and wedges, including diffraction effects.
The physical theory of diffraction uses equivalent edge currents on wedges to model scattering from edges.
RECOTA uses Gordon's method to compute integrals over facets for scattered electric fields.
The code includes a shadowing algorithm that turns off contributions from facets or wedges covered by shadow zones.
Multiple scattering contributions are added using a generalized form of Knott's calculations for dihedral corners.
RECOTA execution time averages about 0.0115 seconds per facet per angle on a VAX 11/785 system.
The paper focuses on monostatic RCS and perfectly conducting bodies; dielectric surfaces and bistatic calculations are planned for future work.
The method of components technique provides more flexibility than body of revolution but yields only coarse RCS estimates due to approximations.
RECOTA's approach improves physical optics predictions for flat plates by adding nonuniform edge currents based on physical theory of diffraction.
The paper presents detailed mathematical formulations for facet and wedge scattering integral equations.
